column2: The fault that lies in killing the unkillable is declared to lie in not killing the killable; this indeed is the limit which one should avoid.
Therefore a king who is sharp should establish his subjects in their own dharma; for devouring one another they would roam like wolves.
The kshatriya in whose realm bands of robbers plunder others' goods like crows taking fish from water is the defiler of his class.
Making well-born ministers endowed with Vedic learning, rule the earth, king, protecting the subjects by dharma.
The king who takes up one low-born and without deeds, ignorant of the difference between the two, makes that kshatra impotent.
Neither the fierce nor the mild is praised here by dharma; one should not transgress either; having become fierce, be mild.
This dharma of the kshatriya is hard; the goodwill that stands in you was created for fierce action; therefore rule the kingdom.
Always restraining the wicked and protecting the good: so the wise Shakra said, in calamities, bull of the Bharatas.
[Yudhishthira said:] "Is there a limit for robbers that another should not transgress? I ask you, best of the good; tell me that, grandsire."
[Bhishma said:] "He should serve only brahmanas, the learned, the aged and the ascetics, rich in learning, conduct and livelihood, for this is the highest purifier.
The conduct you have toward the gods, let it always be so toward brahmanas; for when brahmanas are angry, king, deeds are done in many ways.
By their favour glory is chief, by their displeasure the reverse; for when pleased, brahmanas are like nectar, and when angry, like poison."
[Bhishma said:] "Great is the dharma, great king, of protecting one who has come for refuge; you are fit to ask the question, best of the Bharatas.
Nriga and other kings, great king, having protected those who came for refuge, attained the highest perfection.
For it is heard that an enemy who came to a pigeon for refuge was honoured as is just, and invited to eat of the pigeon's own flesh."
[Yudhishthira said:] "How, in former times, did an enemy come to a pigeon for refuge and get fed with its own flesh, and what end did he reach, Bharata?"
[Bhishma said:] "Hear, king, the divine tale that destroys all sin, told by Bhargava to King Muchukunda.
Of old, Partha, King Muchukunda bowed and asked Bhargava about this very matter, bull of the Bharatas.
To him, listening eagerly, Bhargava told the tale of how perfection was gained by a pigeon, lord of men.
Hear, attentive, king, mighty-armed, as I tell the tale, joined with the determination of dharma and bearing on desire and wealth.
He had no friend, no relative, no kinsman; for he had been abandoned by them for that dreadful deed.
Taking his snare, he killed birds in the forest always, and sold those flying creatures, lord of men.
As that evil-souled man lived thus by his trade, a very long time passed, and he did not understand the adharma.
His wife was his companion, and, delighting in her ever, bewildered by the working of fate, he liked no other livelihood.
Then once, as he was in the forest, a great storm of wind arose, as though felling those trees.
In a good moment the sky, crowded with clouds and adorned with rings of lightning, was covered, like a sea by a ship's place.
Delighted, with masses of streaming rain, the lord of a hundred sacrifices filled the earth with water in a moment.
Then, with the world full of downpours, confused and senseless, tormented by cold, he wandered all that forest with a troubled heart.
The bird-killer found neither low ground nor high ground, for the path of that forest was filled with floods of water.
Birds, struck by the force of the wind, lay hidden then; deer, lions and boars took shelter on dry ground and stayed.
Terrified by the great wind and rain, those forest-dwellers, afflicted by fear and hunger, wandered about together in the forest.
But he, his limbs struck by the cold, walked on and did not stop; in the groves he saw a tree dark as a cloud.
The sky, rich in stars, like a night-lotus and spotless, was free of clouds; seeing it, the fowler, shaking with cold,
looked about the directions, and the hour; the evil-minded man saw that the village lay far from that place, lord, and resolved to spend that night in that forest.
With folded hands, restrained, he spoke to the tree: "I take refuge in whatever deities are in this tree, Bharata."
Laying his head on a stone and spreading leaves on the ground, filled with great misery, the bird-killer then slept.
His wife, gone out at dawn, had not returned to feed; seeing the night come, that bird was tormented.

There has been a great wind and rain, and my beloved has not come; what is the reason that she has not returned even now?
mahabharata:12:142.4	May my beloved be safe in the forest; without her my house is empty today.
mahabharata:12:142.5	If that wife with red-cornered eyes, speckled body and sweet voice does not come to me today, I have no use for life.
mahabharata:12:142.6	Devoted to her husband's dharma, virtuous, dearer than life, that ascetic one knows me weary and hungry.
mahabharata:12:142.7	Loving, benevolent, tender and devoted: the man who has such a wife is blessed on earth.
mahabharata:12:142.8	A wife is said here to be a man's greatest protector; for one without helpers in this world, she helps the course of life.
mahabharata:12:142.9	For one overcome by disease and ever in hardship, there is no remedy for an afflicted man like a wife.
As the afflicted bird lamented thus, the wife, caught by the fowler, heard his words.
She is not a wife in speech whose husband is not pleased; with fire as witness, the husband is a woman's refuge.
Thus reflecting, grieving, the she-pigeon, held by the fowler, spoke to her sorrowing husband.

Well, I shall tell you your good, and hearing it, do so: be especially a protector of one who has come for refuge, beloved.
mahabharata:12:142.15	This fowler lies here, having come to your dwelling, afflicted by cold and hunger; show him honour.
mahabharata:12:142.16	Whoever kills a twice-born, or a cow, the mother of the world, or one who has come for refuge, the sin of these is equal.
mahabharata:12:142.17	The livelihood prescribed for us by the dharma of our kind, that of pigeons, is rightly followed ever by one such as you with self-control.
mahabharata:12:142.18	We have heard that the householder who follows dharma as he is able gains imperishable worlds after death.
mahabharata:12:142.19	You today have offspring and a son, twice-born; setting aside concern for your own body, and taking up dharma and wealth, show him honour so that his mind is pleased.
Thus the she-bird in the snare, the ascetic, spoke, greatly afflicted, and looked at her husband.
Hearing his wife's words, joined with the logic of dharma, filled with great joy, his eyes full of tears,
seeing the fowler, the bird honoured, with effort, by the rite seen in scripture, that man who lived on birds.
And he said, "Welcome; tell me what I should do; do not grieve; you are in your own house.
Tell me quickly what I should do, what you wish; I speak to you with affection, for you have come to us for refuge.
Hospitality is to be done with effort to one who has come for refuge, especially by a householder engaged in the five sacrifices.
The householder who out of delusion does not perform the five sacrifices has by dharma neither this world nor the next.
So tell me, trusting; whatever you say in words I shall do, all of it; do not turn your mind against the world."
Hearing the bird's words, the fowler said, "The cold afflicts me; let a protection from the frost be made."
Thus addressed, the bird spread leaves on the ground and went quickly to fetch dry ones with effort, for kindling.
Going to a place where charcoal was made, he took fire and came back, and then kindled the fire in the dry leaves.
Having made a great blaze, he said to him who had come for refuge, "Warm yourself, trusting, and your limbs, without fear from any quarter."
Thus addressed, he said "so be it," and the fowler warmed his limbs; his life restored by the fire, he then spoke to the bird.
I want food to be given; hunger torments me. Promising that, the bird spoke.

I have no store by which I might end your hunger; we forest-dwellers live ever on what arises.
mahabharata:12:142.35	We have no hoard, like the sages in the forest. Having said this, he then became pale-faced.
How indeed should it be done? he was ever absorbed in this thought, best of the Bharatas, reproaching his own livelihood.
After a moment, regaining consciousness, the bird said to the bird-killer, "I shall satisfy you; wait a moment."
Having said this, he kindled a fire with dry leaves, and the pigeon, filled with great joy, spoke again.

I have heard before of the dharma of gods, sages, ancestors and great souls: great is the honouring of a guest.
mahabharata:12:142.40	Show me favour today; I tell you this truth; my mind is made up about the honouring of a guest.
Then that bird, true to his promise, as if laughing, circled the fire three times and entered it, lord of the earth.
Seeing the bird enter the midst of the fire, the fowler thought in his mind, "What have I done?
Alas, for me, cruel and despised for my own deeds, a great and dreadful adharma will come, without doubt."
Thus the fowler lamented in many ways, reproaching his own deeds, seeing the bird in such a state.
What a thing I, cruel and senseless, have done! The sin will remain always in my heart as long as I live.
Reproaching himself again and again, he said, "Shame on me, of evil mind, ever resolved on deceit, who gave up good deeds to be a fowler of birds.
This is a rebuke to me, cruel as I am, without doubt, given by the great-souled pigeon, who gave his own flesh.
I shall give up my dear life, leaving my wife and sons; for dharma has been taught to me by the pigeon, so supremely righteous.
From today I shall dry up my body, deprived of all enjoyments, as a little water dries in summer.
Enduring hunger, thirst and heat, thin, with veins showing, I shall practise by many fasts what bears on the next world.

Ah, by giving his body he showed the honouring of a guest; therefore I shall practise dharma, for dharma is the highest goal; dharma has been seen by the most righteous in the form of this best of birds."
Having spoken thus and resolved, the fowler of dreadful deeds, of strict vows, took the great departure and set out.

[The she-pigeon said:] "Beloved, I do not remember ever having displeased you. Every woman who is a widow, though with many sons, bird, is to be pitied by her kin, if she is high-minded and without a husband.
I was always cherished by you, honoured, and comforted with sweet, tender and charming words again and again.
In mountain caves, by river waterfalls, and on lovely treetops, I was delighted by you, my dear.
In travelling through the sky, too, I was happy with you; I have roamed with you, beloved; today I have nothing.
A father gives a measure, a mother a measure, a son a measure; who would not honour a husband, the giver of the measureless?
There is no protector like a husband, no happiness like a husband; leaving aside all wealth, the husband is a woman's refuge.
I have no use for life here without you, lord; what virtuous woman, even if without a husband, could bear to live?"
Having lamented thus in many pitiful ways, that wife, devoted to her husband and sorely grieved, entered the blazing fire.
By what austerity could I reach the highest goal? Having determined this by thought, he began to set out.
The fowler, who lived by birds, having taken the great departure, motionless, living on air, without possessiveness, in desire of heaven,
then saw a very wide, delightful lake adorned with lotuses, crowded with flocks of various birds, with cool, fair water; even one thirsty, seeing it, would be sated, without doubt.
Emaciated by fasting, the fowler, king, joyfully went on to the forest inhabited by wild beasts.
Having made a great resolve, the fowler entered, and as he entered the forest he was seized by thorns.
His limbs torn by thorns, his skin wet with blood, he wandered in that lonely place full of many deer.
Then in the forest, by the wind among the great trees, a mighty fire arose from the friction.
The fire, enraged, burned that forest, thick with trees and tangled with creepers and branches, with a blaze like the fire at the end of the age.
Then, with a joyful heart, for release of his body, the fowler ran toward the swelling fire.
Burnt by that fire, the fowler, his sins destroyed, then reached the highest perfection, best of the Bharatas.
Then, free of fever, he saw himself in heaven, shining like Indra among yakshas, gandharvas and siddhas.
Thus indeed the pigeon and the devoted she-pigeon went to heaven with the fowler, by meritorious deeds.
And any woman who so follows her husband shines at once, standing in heaven like the she-pigeon.
So this is the old tale of the great-souled fowler and the pigeon, whose end was most righteous through meritorious deeds.
Whoever hears this always, or recites it, has nothing inauspicious, even in mind, though heedless.

Yudhishthira, this dharma is great, best of those who uphold dharma: even for killers of cows there may be atonement for the sinful deed, but there is none for one who kills one who has come for refuge."
[Bhishma said:] "Here I shall relate to you an ancient tale, what the brahmana Indrota Shaunaka said to Janamejaya.
There was a king, Janamejaya son of Parikshit, of great valour; the sin of brahmin-slaying, committed unwittingly, came upon that lord of the earth.
All the brahmanas and his priests abandoned him; the king went to the forest, burning day and night.
Abandoned by his subjects, he did much good; he performed austerity to excess, burning with remorse.
Here I shall tell the tale that supports this dharma: Janamejaya, burning with the sin of his deed, went
to choose Indrota Shaunaka, of strict vows; approaching him, he clasped his feet, pressing them.
Then the greatly wise one, afraid, rebuked him sharply: "You are the doer of a great sin, a slayer of a brahmin; why have you come here?
What is to be done by you with us? Do not ask me in any way; go, go; for your place here will surely not please us.
Your life is in vain, king, and you live in torment; you were created for sin and for the lowest deeds here.
Fathers strive for sons wishing them much good, by austerity, by worship of gods, by salutation and forbearance.
See this line of ancestors gone to hell because of you; all their hopes and bonds that rested on you are in vain.
Those whom people honour and gain heaven, long life, fame and happiness, toward those brahmanas your hatred is constant and pointless.
Leaving this world, you will fall head downward, for unending years, by your sinful deed.
Eaten by vultures, blue-throated birds and iron-mouthed creatures, from there again you will return and go to a sinful womb.
If you think, king, "there is no other world," where then? The messengers of Yama will remind you in Yama's abode."
[Janamejaya said:] "Shame on the deed, shame on me who did it; therefore I seek to appease you; all this is of my own making; I burn as if set in a fire.
Reflecting on my own deeds, my mind takes no joy; I have surely met a dreadful fear, even from Vaivasvata.
How shall I live without drawing out that thorn? Putting away all anger, Shaunaka, speak to me.
I shall again become a provider of food for brahmanas, and have purpose; let some remnant of this family remain; let this family not be defeated.
For we, cursed by brahmanas, can have no remnant, for those who do not obtain the Vedas know it for certain.
Greatly despondent, I shall speak further now; and again they perish, those without dharma and without recitation.
They settle down on this side, like Pulindas and Shabaras; for those without sacrifice never reach the other world in any way.
Without knowing my wisdom, like a wise man toward a child, brahmana, like a father toward his sons, Shaunaka, wish me well."
He gets no benefit there and sees no tasks, his soul despondent, or he is unseen, scorned by all the good.
Knowing the power on both sides, and the greatness in the Veda and tradition, perform here a great pacifying rite; let Brahma be your refuge.
That is the lovely thing for the next world; let the brahmanas not be angry; if you are tormented by sin and see dharma,
[Janamejaya said:] "I repent of the sin and do not practise adharma; I long for one who seeks prosperity and serves, Shaunaka."
[Shaunaka said:] "Cutting off stiffness and pride, I wish for affection from you, king; abide in the good of all beings, and remember dharma.
I summon you neither from fear, nor from meanness, nor from greed; let the gods hear that true speech of mine with the brahmanas.
I want nothing from anyone, and I summon you to dharma, while all beings cry out, saying 'Shame!'
Those ignorant of dharma will speak of me, unfriendly people will speak; hearing those words, my friends will burn greatly.
Only a few of great wisdom will understand the purpose; know what I have done, dear, toward brahmanas, Bharata.
Do so that they gain welfare through me; and promise, king, that you will do no injury to brahmanas."
[Janamejaya said:] "Never by speech, nor mind, nor deed again shall I harm brahmanas; I touch your feet, brahmana."
[Shaunaka said:] "Beings favour one another by their own conduct, king; the world surely decides that everything is good and bad, where you, being such, now look to dharma.
That one, leaving delicious food and enjoyments, has taken up austerity: this too is a wonder among beings, Janamejaya.
They say it is no wonder if a giver is weak or a poor man is rich in austerity; for it is not far off.
This very thing is wholly meanness, unexamined; therefore it should be by examination alone that virtue arises in it.
Sacrifice, giving, compassion, the Vedas and truth, lord of the earth: these five are purifiers, and sixth, good conduct and austerity.
That alone is the supreme purifier of kings, Janamejaya; by rightly taking it up you will gain the higher dharma.
Going to holy places is held to be a supreme purifier; and these verses sung by Yayati are cited here.
The mortal who should undertake it, or who would live again, having performed a sacrifice wholly, renouncing it should practise austerity.
The great asura... Pushkara, Prabhasa, Uttara Manasa, Kalodaka: you will go to these, with life regained and living again.
Serve and follow the Sarasvati and the Drishadvati; devoted to study, bathe at all the sacred places.
He called renunciation the dharma of giving up the highest of purifiers; here too are cited these verses made by Satyavat.
As a young boy is truthful, neither meritorious nor a doer of sin; there is no sorrow in all beings here; whence happiness here?
Thus, for beings in their natural state, going through all contacts, giving up life, virtue and sin are laid open.
But what is higher than all tasks for a king, that I tell you: win heaven by strength and by sharing, and purify yourself.
The man who has such strength and vigour is lord of dharma; for the happiness of brahmanas, go about this earth.
As you formerly insulted them, so now appease them; even if scorned and abandoned in many ways,
the sight of oneself, learned one: "I am not a killer," do not be angry; striving in your own tasks, do what is supremely good.
Some king is like frost and terrible fire, another like a plough and thunderbolt, scourge of foes.
One should not think of oneself as wholly beyond cure, nor ever be attached, thinking "I am not that," to the wicked.
One tormented by a wrongful deed is freed from a quarter of the sin; by "this must not be done again," from a second; by "I shall practise dharma alone," from a third.
A man wishing to prosper should approve what is good; those who serve the fragrant become fragrant, and those who serve the foul-smelling become so.
One given to austerity is at once freed from sin; one accused is freed by tending the fire a year; the killer of a brahmin is freed by tending the fire three years.
By releasing from death as many living beings as he has killed, of the same kind, the killer of a brahmin is freed.
Or let him plunge in water thrice muttering the Aghamarshana; Manu said that it is like the bath of the horse sacrifice.
It quickly drives away sin and he gains honour; and beings are pleased with him, though dull and mute.

The gods and asuras all together approached Brihaspati, the teacher of the gods, king, and questioned him: "You know the fruit in dharma done, great sage, and likewise in the other, the hell of sinful worlds.
But when both good deeds are present in one, which of them would be the higher victory? Tell us the fruit of action, great sage: how does a man of virtue drive away sin?"
[Brihaspati said:] "He who, having done sin before unintentionally, does meritorious deeds intentionally, being of virtuous nature, drives away that sin, as a soiled cloth is cleaned with alkali.
Having done sin, a man should not think "I am not that"; he should wish to do good, with faith and without envy.
He who, being good, opens the rents as of a garment, the man who, having done sin, turns to the good,
as the sun, rising again, dispels all darkness, so the one who practises good dispels all sin."
[Bhishma said:] "Having spoken thus to King Janamejaya, Indrota Shaunaka had him perform the horse sacrifice according to rule.
Then that king, his sin removed, endowed with splendour like blazing fire, the destroyer of foes, entered his own kingdom, like the full-bodied moon the sky."
Some, grieving, took up a boy not yet come to youth, the whole wealth of the family, weeping, overwhelmed with sorrow.
Having taken the dead boy, they stood facing the cremation ground, and passing him from lap to lap they wept on the ground.
At the sound of their weeping a vulture came up and said: "Leave this lone one in the world and go; do not delay.
Here, thousands of men and thousands of women have been brought together by time; were they ever without kin?
See the whole world ruled by pleasures and pains; union and separation come in turn.
Those who take the dead and go, and those who follow, even they go by the measure of their own lifespan, as creatures.
Enough of staying in this cremation ground, crowded with vultures and jackals, full of skeletons, dreadful, terrifying to all creatures.
No one who has met the law of time lives again, whether dear or hated; such is the end of creatures.
With the world ordered by the ending of deeds, and the sun going to its setting, go to your own dwelling, leaving your affection for the son."
Then, hearing the vulture's words, wailing, king, those kinsmen set off, leaving the son on the ground.
Having resolved, abandoning their own child, hopeless of his life, they climbed onto the road and stood.
A jackal, in colour like a crow or a cloud, came out of its hole and said to them as they were leaving: "Humans are indeed pitiless.
The sun is still up, fools; show affection; do not be afraid; a moment has many forms, and he may even live.
You, having laid your son on the ground, bereft of love for him, leaving him in the cremation ground, why do you go, pitiless ones?
You have no affection for this son, a child of sweet speech, by whose mere speech you come to joy.
You do not see the affection for sons that beasts and birds have, from whom no one gets any fruit by keeping them.
Four-footed creatures, birds, insects, beings bound by affection, whose station is in the next world, like the rites of the sages' sacrifices,
for those who delight in sons, no merit is seen here or hereafter, and yet they sustain their offspring.
Not seeing their dear sons, their grief does not last; and when grown they never support their mother and father.
Where is affection among men, whose grief will be so great? How will you go, leaving this son, the founder of your line?
Weep long, and look long with love; such dear ones are hard to give up, especially.
Where kinsmen stay for one who is weak, beset, and facing the cremation ground, no other remains there.
Life is dear to all, and all find affection; see, even among animal wombs, what affection the good have."
[Yudhishthira said:] "I wish to hear more, king, joined with dharma and wealth, as you tell it; you should explain something of that to me."
His son surpassed his father in virtue: Marutta by name, a knower of dharma, an emperor of great fame.
For you are the best of upholders of dharma, ever fond of dharma; a king is the teacher of living beings; therefore I say this.
But they, intoxicated with drink and urged on by anger, struck Yuyudhana then with the leavings of vessels.

[Yudhishthira said:] "Taking back what was given to one who came for refuge, killing a woman, seizing a brahmana's property, and treachery to a friend: these four, Shakra, and abandoning a devotee, I hold to be equal."
Dharma himself, embodied, came to look upon the king, to where that king of the Kurus, Yudhishthira, was.
